item.title: Approximation of adelic divisors and equidistribution of small points
item.headline: When algebraic points settle into a predictable pattern
item.summary: Solutions to polynomial equations can have surprisingly orderly collective behavior. This paper extends a theorem about how families of related algebraic points spread out as their arithmetic height approaches a minimum. Height measures arithmetic complexity, not distance from the origin. The new theorem allows more flexible height functions than an earlier general result, provided a precise approximation condition holds. It predicts a limiting distribution, which need not be uniform in ordinary space; it does not say that every collection of simple-looking numbers behaves this way.

evidence.question: When do Galois orbits of algebraic points approaching the essential minimum of a height function converge to a common distribution?
evidence.method: Mathematical proof using semipositive approximations of adelic divisors, a variational principle and a refined arithmetic Siu inequality. Error estimates controlled by a geometric quantity called the inradius establish differentiability of the essential minimum, yielding equidistribution.
evidence.limitations: Requires a big underlying divisor, the stated approximation condition and a generic sequence whose heights approach the essential minimum. The condition is not automatic. Its necessity is established in particular settings, not in complete generality.

explainer.finding: The authors prove a more flexible condition ensuring that the algebraically related companions of low-height points approach the same probability distribution. Their result covers cases excluded by an equality required in Yuan's earlier theorem.
explainer.method: They approximate a difficult arithmetic object by better-behaved ones and tightly control the errors. A variational argument then connects changes in the minimum height to the limiting distribution. This is a proof, not a simulation or a survey of numerical examples.
explainer.meaning: For a picture of the idea, consider the complex solutions of z raised to the nth power equals 1: they sit at evenly spaced positions on a circle. That familiar example is not the new discovery. The paper broadens the conditions under which much more general algebraic families have a predictable limiting pattern.
explainer.limits: Small means low arithmetic height, not close together on a plot. Generic sequences must eventually avoid every fixed proper algebraic subvariety. The theorem also needs its approximation condition; the limiting pattern need not be a uniform spread, and the result does not provide a universal finite-sample error bound.
